::: {.visual-intro}
A language model uses the same weights across languages. If an edit makes the model worse at predicting
the next token in German, how much of that damage carries over to Dutch?

Lucius Bushnaq weakened German predictions by editing one subcomponent in
[Goodfire's four-layer, 67-million-parameter model](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters).
I used the same model and decomposition to test German–Dutch, Spanish–Portuguese and French–Italian.
[Bushnaq's experiment](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ieoWstubDQWLrMnhH/exploration-fine-tuning-with-parameter-decomposition)

On new text, the subcomponent edits did less damage to the related languages than the three comparators.
LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning kept English predictions closer to the original model's.
:::

## Edit one rank-one subcomponent

Goodfire's adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) expresses a weight matrix $W$ as a sum of
**rank-one subcomponents** and a residual. The training objective favors using few subcomponents to
approximate the computation for each input.

A subcomponent $A=u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top$ reads one number from the input $x$ with
$v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x$. That number scales the output vector $u_{\mathrm{out}}$.

$$
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
$$

The edit scales $A$ by a single coefficient $c$, changing many weights at once.

$$
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
$$

At $c=1$ the matrix is unchanged, at $c=0$ the contribution is removed, and at $c<0$ its sign reverses.

## Compare edits at similar target damage {#comparing-ways-to-change-the-weights}

The selector ranks subcomponents by how much a small coefficient change is predicted to raise target
loss for a given change in English predictions. It tests leading candidates on target training text.
The comparison included three other ways to worsen target predictions while preserving English.

- **Rank-one LoRA** learns a new pair of input and output vectors for the same matrix as the VPD edit.
- **Full-matrix fine-tuning** can change every entry in the 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.
- **Neuron edits** reduce output weights for neurons that activate more often on target text than on English.

<span id="matching-the-intended-damage"></span>An edit could spare Dutch by barely affecting German. Calibration sets the strength of each edit to
raise mean next-token prediction loss (cross-entropy) by **0.5 or 1 nat/token** on target-language
validation text.

The final comparison used the fixed edits on text from **58 held-out European Parliament session dates**.
The related languages were absent from selection and training for these runs. In earlier work I used
development text from those languages and took Dutch performance into account when choosing the German subcomponent.
[Data and prior access](index.qmd#sec-access)

Related-language loss rose by **0.0003–0.0053 nat/token** across the six fixed VPD edits in this model,
versus **0.027–0.876 nat/token** across individual comparator runs. The selection rule's reliability
on new tasks remains open. [Estimates and confidence intervals](index.qmd#sec-contrasts)

## How much did English predictions change? {#what-changed-in-english}

All edits in the main comparison passed the English loss limit. That loss uses the probability of the
observed next token. **KL divergence** compares the full next-token distributions of the original and
edited models. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning penalized English KL during training. In the post hoc
analysis, both had lower English KL than VPD for every language and calibration level on the new dates.

```{=html}
<figure class="visual-figure" aria-label="English prediction change relative to the original model">
  <div id="visual-english-interactive" hidden>
    <div class="visual-controls">
      <label for="visual-english-pair">Target language
        <select id="visual-english-pair"><option value="de">German</option><option value="es">Spanish</option><option value="fr">French</option></select>
      </label>
      <fieldset class="visual-dose"><legend>Target loss increase on validation text</legend>
        <button type="button" data-visual-tau="0.5" aria-pressed="false">0.5 nat/token</button>
        <button type="button" data-visual-tau="1" aria-pressed="true">1 nat/token</button>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div id="visual-english-chart"></div>
    <details class="visual-uncertainty-table">
      <summary>Read the plotted values</summary>
      <div id="visual-english-table"></div>
    </details>
  </div>
  <div id="visual-english-fallback">
    <p>See the <a href="index.html#sec-english">paper's English comparison</a> for the measurements for all four methods.</p>
  </div>
  <figcaption id="visual-english-caption"><span class="plot-key">Lines span the three training subsets. KL is measured from the original model to the edited model.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
```

Mean English KL was below **0.001 nat/token** for every VPD edit. For scale, the KL from a fair coin
(**50%/50%**) to a **52%/48%** coin is about **0.00080**. The German VPD edit at the 1 nat/token
level had a mean KL of **0.00077**. Individual contexts can have higher KL than the mean.
